column1: {"title": "Explanation in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Social Sciences"
column2: "abstract": "There has been a recent resurgence in the area of explainable artificial intelligence as researchers and practitioners seek to make their algorithms more understandable. Much of this research is focused on explicitly explaining decisions or actions to a human observer
column3: and it should not be controversial to say that looking at how humans explain to each other can serve as a useful starting point for explanation in artificial intelligence. However
column4: it is fair to say that most work in explainable artificial intelligence uses only the researchers' intuition of what constitutes a `good' explanation. There exists vast and valuable bodies of research in philosophy
column5: psychology
column6: and cognitive science of how people define
column7: generate
column8: select
column9: evaluate
column10: and present explanations
column11: which argues that people employ certain cognitive biases and social expectations towards the explanation process. This paper argues that the field of explainable artificial intelligence should build on this existing research
column12: and reviews relevant papers from philosophy
column15: which study these topics. It draws out some important findings
column16: and discusses ways that these can be infused with work on explainable artificial intelligence."

column1: {"title": "Exploring the Effects of User-Agent and User-Designer Similarity in Virtual Human Design to Promote Mental Health Intentions for College Students"
column2: "abstract": "Virtual humans (i.e.

column4: particularly in Science
column5: Technology

column7: and Mathematics (STEM) fields where students are at a heightened risk of mental disorders such as anxiety and depression. A comprehensive understanding of students

column9: experiences

column11: is crucial for creating timely and effective virtual human interventions. To this end

Key factors influencing virtual human design included age

column1: {"title": "GazeFusion: Saliency-Guided Image Generation"
column2: "abstract": "Diffusion models offer unprecedented image generation power given just a text prompt. While emerging approaches for controlling diffusion models have enabled users to specify the desired spatial layouts of the generated content
column3: they cannot predict or control where viewers will pay more attention due to the complexity of human vision. Recognizing the significance of attention-controllable image generation in practical applications
column4: we present a saliency-guided framework to incorporate the data priors of human visual attention mechanisms into the generation process. Given a user-specified viewer attention distribution
column5: our control module conditions a diffusion model to generate images that attract viewers’ attention toward the desired regions. To assess the efficacy of our approach
column6: we performed an eye-tracked user study and a large-scale model-based saliency analysis. The results evidence that both the cross-user eye gaze distributions and the saliency models’ predictions align with the desired attention distributions. Lastly
column7: we outline several applications
column8: including interactive design of saliency guidance
column9: attention suppression in unwanted regions
column10: and adaptive generation for varied display/viewing conditions."

column1: {"title": "Multi-Objective Optimization for Multi-UAV-Assisted Mobile Edge Computing"
column2: "abstract": "Recent developments in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and mobile edge computing (MEC) have provided users with flexible and resilient computing services. However
column3: meeting the computation-intensive and delay-sensitive demands of users poses a significant challenge due to the limited resources of UAVs. To address this challenge
column4: we consider a multi-UAV-assisted MEC system. Based on this system
column5: we formulate a multi-objective optimization problem aiming at minimizing the total task completion delay
column6: reducing the total UAV energy consumption
column7: and maximizing the total number of offloaded tasks. Since the problem is a mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) and NP-hard problem
column8: we propose a joint task offloading
column9: computation resource allocation
column10: and UAV trajectory control (JTORATC) approach. The problem is split into three components to cope with the coupling of these decision variables
column11: and then solved individually to obtain the corresponding decisions. Specifically
column12: the sub-problem of task offloading is solved by using distributed splitting and threshold rounding methods
column13: the sub-problem of computation resource allocation is solved by adopting the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) method
column14: and the sub-problem of UAV trajectory control is solved by employing the successive convex approximation (SCA) method. Simulation results show that the proposed JTORATC has superior performance compared with the other benchmark methods."

column1: {"title": "Generative AI for Self-Adaptive Systems: State of the Art and Research Roadmap"
column2: "abstract": "Self-adaptive systems (SASs) are designed to handle changes and uncertainties through a feedback loop with four core functionalities: monitoring
column3: analyzing
column4: planning
column5: and execution. Recently
column6: generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)
column7: especially the area of large language models
column8: has shown impressive performance in data comprehension and logical reasoning. These capabilities are highly aligned with the functionalities required in SASs
column9: suggesting a strong potential to employ GenAI to enhance SASs. However
column10: the specific benefits and challenges of employing GenAI in SASs remain unclear. Yet
column11: providing a comprehensive understanding of these benefits and challenges is complex due to several reasons: limited publications in the SAS field
column12: the technological and application diversity within SASs
column13: and the rapid evolution of GenAI technologies. To that end
column14: this article aims to provide researchers and practitioners a comprehensive snapshot that outlines the potential benefits and challenges of employing GenAI’s within SAS. Specifically
column17: and analyze literature from four distinct research fields and organize them into two main categories to potential benefits: (i) enhancements to the autonomy of SASs centered around the specific functions of the MAPE-K feedback loop
column18: and (ii) improvements in the interaction between humans and SASs within human-on-the-loop settings. From our study
column19: we outline a research roadmap that highlights the challenges of integrating GenAI into SASs. The roadmap starts with outlining key research challenges that need to be tackled to exploit the potential for applying GenAI in the field of SAS. The roadmap concludes with a practical reflection

column1: {"title": "A User Study on Explainable Online Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Systems"

column1: {"title": "Dynamic Reliability Management in Neuromorphic Computing"
column2: "abstract": "Neuromorphic computing systems execute machine learning tasks designed with spiking neural networks. These systems are embracing non-volatile memory to implement high-density and low-energy synaptic storage. Elevated voltages and currents needed to operate non-volatile memories cause aging of CMOS-based transistors in each neuron and synapse circuit in the hardware
column3: drifting the transistor’s parameters from their nominal values. If these circuits are used continuously for too long
column4: the parameter drifts cannot be reversed
column5: resulting in permanent degradation of circuit performance over time
column6: eventually leading to hardware faults. Aggressive device scaling increases power density and temperature
column7: which further accelerates the aging
column8: challenging the reliable operation of neuromorphic systems. Existing reliability-oriented techniques periodically de-stress all neuron and synapse circuits in the hardware at fixed intervals
column9: assuming worst-case operating conditions
column10: without actually tracking their aging at run-time. To de-stress these circuits
column11: normal operation must be interrupted
column12: which introduces latency in spike generation and propagation
column13: impacting the inter-spike interval and hence
column15: accuracy). We observe that in contrast to long-term aging
column17: short-term aging in scaled CMOS transistors is mostly due to bias temperature instability. The latter is heavily workload-dependent and
column19: partially reversible. We propose a new architectural technique to mitigate the aging-related reliability problems in neuromorphic systems by designing an intelligent run-time manager (NCRTM)
column20: which dynamically de-stresses neuron and synapse circuits in response to the short-term aging in their CMOS transistors during the execution of machine learning workloads
column21: with the objective of meeting a reliability target. NCRTM de-stresses these circuits only when it is absolutely necessary to do so
column22: otherwise reducing the performance impact by scheduling de-stress operations off the critical path. We evaluate NCRTM with state-of-the-art machine learning workloads on a neuromorphic hardware. Our results demonstrate that NCRTM significantly improves the reliability of neuromorphic hardware

column1: {"title": "NORM: An FPGA-based Non-volatile Memory Emulation Framework for Intermittent Computing"
column2: "abstract": "Today’s intermittent computing systems operate by relying only on harvested energy accumulated in their tiny energy reservoirs
column3: typically capacitors. An intermittent device dies due to a power failure when there is no energy in its capacitor and boots again when the harvested energy is sufficient to power its hardware components. Power failures prevent the forward progress of computation due to the frequent loss of computational state. To remedy this problem
column4: intermittent computing systems comprise built-in fast non-volatile memories with high write endurance to store information that persists despite frequent power failures. However
column5: the lack of design tools makes fast-prototyping these systems difficult. Even though FPGAs are common platforms for fast prototyping and behavioral verification of continuously powered architectures
column6: they do not target prototyping intermittent computing systems. This article introduces a new FPGA-based framework
column7: named NORM (Non-volatile memORy eMulator)
column8: to emulate and verify the behavior of any intermittent computing system that exploits fast non-volatile memories. Our evaluation showed that NORM can be used to emulate and validate FeRAM-based transiently powered hardware architectures successfully."

column1: {"title": "Fair-RGNN: Mitigating Relational Bias on Knowledge Graphs"
column2: "abstract": "Knowledge graph data are prevalent in real-world applications
column3: and knowledge graph neural networks (KGNNs) are essential techniques for knowledge graph representation learning. Although KGNN effectively models the structural information from knowledge graphs
column4: these frameworks amplify the underlying data bias that leads to discrimination towards certain groups or individuals in resulting applications. Additionally
column5: as existing debiasing approaches mainly focus on entity-wise bias
column6: eliminating the multi-hop relational bias that pervasively exists in knowledge graphs remains an open question. However
column7: it is very challenging to eliminate relational bias due to the sparsity of the paths that generate the bias and the non-linear proximity structure of knowledge graphs. To tackle the challenges
column8: we propose Fair-KGNN
column9: a KGNN framework that simultaneously alleviates multi-hop bias and preserves the proximity information of entity-to-relation in knowledge graphs. The proposed framework is generalizable to mitigate relational bias for all types of KGNN. Fair-KGNN is applicable to incorporate two state-of-the-art KGNN models

column11: to mitigate gender-occupation and nationality-salary bias. The experiments carried out on three benchmark knowledge graph datasets demonstrate that Fair-KGNN can effectively mitigate unfair situations during representation learning while preserving the predictive performance of KGNN models. The source code of the proposed method is available at: https://github.com/ynchuang/Mitigating-Relational-Bias-on-Knowledge-Graphs."

column1: {"title": "Enhancing Heterogeneous Knowledge Graph Completion with a Novel GAT-based Approach"

column10: enabling the robust performance of GATH in scenarios with imbalanced samples. Comprehensive experiments are conducted to evaluate GATH’s performance. Compared with the existing state-of-the-art GAT-based model on Hits@10 and MRR metrics

column2: "abstract": "Neural graphics primitives

column1: {"title": "MoVer: Motion Verification for Motion Graphics Animations"
column2: "abstract": "While large vision-language models can generate motion graphics animations from text prompts
column3: they regularly fail to include all spatio-temporal properties described in the prompt. We introduce MoVer
column4: a motion verification DSL based on first-order logic that can check spatio-temporal properties of a motion graphics animation. We identify a general set of such properties that people commonly use to describe animations (e.g.
column5: the direction and timing of motions
column6: the relative positioning of objects
column7: etc.). We implement these properties as predicates in MoVer and provide an execution engine that can apply a MoVer program to any input SVG-based motion graphics animation. We then demonstrate how MoVer can be used in an LLM-based synthesis and verification pipeline for iteratively refining motion graphics animations. Given a text prompt

column9: focus on performance with little to no concern for security. This increases the exposure of the open FH to security risks. Attacks targeting synchronization mechanisms pose significant threats
column10: potentially disrupting 5G networks and impairing connectivity. In this article

column3: yet traditional approaches often suffer from high computational costs or limited detection capabilities. Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in code understanding
column4: but their deployment for vulnerability detection is hindered by significant resource requirements. The proposed approach integrates structural code features extracted from abstract syntax trees and control flow graphs with semantic features derived from lightweight LLM embeddings
column5: capturing both the syntactic and semantic aspects of code. A feature fusion mechanism is designed to combine these heterogeneous features effectively
column6: enabling the detection model to identify vulnerability patterns across different codebases. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the lightweight LLM-based approach achieves competitive or superior performance compared to heavyweight models while requiring substantially less computational resources
column7: making it suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments."

column1: {"title": "Applying bayesian data analysis for causal inference about requirements quality: a controlled experiment"
column2: "abstract": "It is commonly accepted that the quality of requirements specifications impacts subsequent software engineering activities. However
column3: we still lack empirical evidence to support organizations in deciding whether their requirements are good enough or impede subsequent activities. column7: ambiguous pronouns lead to incorrect associations in domain models. Despite being equally advised against by literature and frequentist methods
column8: the Bayesian data analysis shows that the two investigated quality defects have vastly different impacts on software engineering activities and

column1: {"title": "Supporting the identification of prevalent quality issues in code changes by analyzing reviewers' feedback"
column2: "abstract": "Context: Code reviewers provide valuable feedback during the code review. Identifying common issues described in the reviewers' feedback can provide input for devising context-specific software development improvements. However
column3: the use of reviewer feedback for this purpose is currently less explored. Objective: In this study
column4: we assess how automation can derive more interpretable and informative themes in reviewers' feedback and whether these themes help to identify recurring quality-related issues in code changes. Method: We conducted a participatory case study using the JabRef system to analyze reviewers' feedback on merged and abandoned code changes. We used two promising topic modeling methods (GSDMM and BERTopic) to identify themes in 5
column5: 560 code review comments. The resulting themes were analyzed and named by a domain expert from JabRef. Results: The domain expert considered the identified themes from the two topic models to represent quality-related issues. Different quality issues are pointed out in code reviews for merged and abandoned code changes. While BERTopic provides higher objective coherence
column6: the domain expert considered themes from short-text topic modeling more informative and easy to interpret than BERTopic-based topic modeling. Conclusions: The identified prevalent code quality issues aim to address the maintainability-focused issues. The analysis of code review comments can enhance the current practices for JabRef by improving the guidelines for new developers and focusing discussions in the developer forums. The topic model choice impacts the interpretability of the generated themes
column7: and a higher coherence (based on objective measures) of generated topics did not lead to improved interpretability by a domain expert."

column1: {"title": "On the correlation between architectural smells and static analysis warnings"
column2: "abstract": "Software quality assurance is essential during software development and maintenance. Static Analysis Tools (SAT) are widely used for assessing code quality. Architectural smells are becoming more daunting to address and evaluate among quality issues. We aim to understand the relationships between Static Analysis Warnings (\"warnings\") and Architectural Smells (\"smell\") to guide developers/maintainers in focusing their effort on warnings more prone to co-occurring with smell. We performed an empirical study on 103 Java projects totaling 72 million LOC belonging to projects from a vast set of domains
column3: and 785 warnings were detected by three SAT

column5: Findbugs
column6: PMD
column7: SonarQube
column8: and 4 architectural smells were detected by the ARCAN tool. We analyzed how warnings influence smell presence. Finally
column9: we proposed a smell remediation effort prioritization based on warning severity and warning proneness to specific smells. Our study reveals a moderate correlation between warnings and smells. Different combinations of SATs and warnings significantly affect smell occurrence
column10: with certain warnings more Likely to co-occur with specific smells. Conversely
column11: 33.79% of warnings are \"non-co-occurring\" with any of the smells in our dataset. This provides an early indicator for potential architectural concerns before resource-intensive architectural analysis is performed. Practitioners can ignore about a third of warnings and focus on those most likely to be associated with smells. Prioritizing smell remediation based on warning severity or warning proneness to specific smells results in effective rankings like those based on smell severity. While not a substitute for specialized tools like ARCAN

column1: {"title": "Feature selection based on multi-perspective dynamic neighbourhood entropy measures in a dynamic neighbourhood rough set"
column2: "abstract": "Neighbourhood rough set (NRS)-based feature selection has been extensively applied in data mining. However
column3: the effectiveness of the NRS model is limited by its reliance on the grid search method to determine the optimal neighbourhood parameter

column8: neutral
column9: and optimistic. Next
column10: the concept of the dynamic neighbourhood rough set (DNRS) model is developed. The most significant feature of this model is its adaptive ability to dynamically update the neighbourhood radius of samples on the basis of the information of their distribution in space
column11: without the necessity of setting neighbourhood parameters artificially. Then
column12: algebraic and information-theoretic views are introduced to propose multi-perspective dynamic neighbourhood entropy measures
column13: which effectively measure the uncertainty of the data. In addition
column14: a nonmonotonic feature selection algorithm based on mutual information is designed to overcome the limitations of feature selection algorithms that rely on monotonic evaluation functions. This algorithm utilizes multi-perspective dynamic neighbourhood entropy measures from a neutral perspective. Finally

column1: {"title": "Improved Online Scheduling with Restarts on a Single Machine"
column2: "abstract": "We consider the problem of minimizing the total completion time on a single online machine using restarts. Although restarts can potentially be very beneficial in the context of online scheduling
column3: there has been relatively little research on this topic up until now. We present a very simple online algorithm which is better than 1.4568-competitive. The basic rule of the algorithm is to run jobs in order of increasing size. For possible restarts

column1: {"title": "Generalized Lipschitz Tracing of Implicit Surfaces"
column2: "abstract": "We present a versatile and robust framework to render implicit surfaces defined by black‐box functions that only provide function value queries. We assume that the input function is locally Lipschitz continuous; however
column3: we presume no prior knowledge of its Lipschitz constants. Our pre‐processing step generates a discrete acceleration structure
column4: a Lipschitz field

column6: then bounding the derivatives of the approximating polynomials. The accuracy of the approximation is controlled by the polynomial degree and the granularity of the spatial resolution used during fitting

column9: the input surface may be represented either procedurally or as an arbitrarily filtered grid of function samples. We query the original implicit representation upon ray trace

column1: {"title": "A point-normal interpolatory subdivision scheme preserving conics"
column2: "abstract": "The use of subdivision schemes in applied and real-world contexts requires the development of conceptually simple algorithms that can be converted into fast and efficient implementation procedures. In the domain of interpolatory subdivision schemes

At the centre of our construction lies a conic fitting algorithm that requires as few as four point-normal pairs for finding new edge points (and associated normals) in a subdivision step. Several numerical results are included to showcase the validity of our algorithm. • We construct a univariate interpolatory subdivision scheme that reproduces conic sections. • It is a geometric subdivision scheme based on point-normal pairs. • We demonstrate our new scheme on several examples."
